LOWER LIMB__Applied / Clinical Anatomy:
Why this matters: lower-limb clinical anatomy is dominated by three themes — a nerve wrapped around a bone (common fibular at the fibular neck), a fracture that starves its own bone (intracapsular neck of femur → avascular necrosis), and a fascial compartment that can strangle its contents. Learn the site → structure → deficit chain and most OSCE and written questions fall out of it.

The sciatic nerve splits above the knee. Its two components — the tibial and common fibular — separate at the apex of the popliteal fossa. A high sciatic lesion mimics a combined tibial + common fibular palsy, but the common fibular part is more often affected (it is more lateral and tethered), so even a “sciatic” injury frequently presents as a foot drop.
Foot Drop, Trendelenburg & the Diagnostic Gaits
👟 Foot drop — Common fibular nerve
  • Loss of dorsiflexion (deep fibular → anterior compartment) and eversion (superficial fibular → lateral compartment)
  • Nerve is subcutaneous at the neck of the fibula → vulnerable to fracture, tight plaster, crossed legs, prolonged squatting
  • Gait: high-stepping (steppage) with a foot-slap; the patient lifts the knee high to clear the toes
  • Sensory: dorsum of foot; deep fibular gives the 1st web space
🚶 Trendelenburg — Superior gluteal nerve
  • Weak gluteus medius & minimus can’t stabilise the pelvis when standing on that leg
  • The pelvis drops on the opposite (unsupported) side — “the sound side sags”
  • The lesion is on the stance (weak) side; bilateral disease → a waddling gait
  • Also seen in hip OA, DDH, and after hip surgery
Deep vs superficial fibular — split the foot drop. A deep fibular lesion loses dorsiflexion (foot drop) + the 1st web space sensation but keeps eversion. A superficial fibular lesion loses eversion + most of the dorsum of the foot but keeps dorsiflexion. Only a common fibular lesion loses both.

Weber classification & the Ottawa rules. Ankle fractures are graded by the level of the fibular fracture relative to the tibiofibular syndesmosis: A = below (stable), B = at the level (variable), C = above (syndesmosis disrupted → unstable). The Ottawa rules decide who needs imaging: the ankle rules → X-ray for tenderness at the posterior edge/tip of either malleolus or inability to weight-bear (4 steps); the foot rules → X-ray for tenderness at the navicular or the base of the 5th metatarsal.
The Hip — Blood Supply, AVN & Dislocation
Femoral head blood supply
  • Chiefly the medial femoral circumflex artery (from profunda femoris) → retinacular vessels ascending the neck under the capsule
  • Lateral femoral circumflex contributes less; the artery of ligamentum teres is minor (mostly relevant in children)
  • An intracapsular neck-of-femur # tears the retinacular vessels → AVN & non-union
  • Displaced intracapsular # → hemiarthroplasty / THR; extracapsular → dynamic hip screw
Hip dislocation & the fractured hip
  • A fractured NOF leg lies shortened & externally rotated
  • Posterior dislocation (~90%) — dashboard injury: limb flexed, adducted, internally rotated & shortened; the sciatic nerve is at risk
  • Anterior dislocation — limb abducted & externally rotated
The Femoral Triangle & Vascular Access
Borders & contents (“NAVEL”)
  • Borders: inguinal ligament (superior), sartorius (lateral), adductor longus (medial); floor = iliopsoas + pectineus
  • Contents lateral→medial: femoral Nerve · Artery · Vein · Empty space (femoral canal) · Lymphatics
  • The nerve lies outside the femoral sheath (which contains artery, vein & canal)
Clinical access & the femoral hernia
  • Femoral pulse at the mid-inguinal point (midway ASIS → pubic symphysis) — site for arterial lines / angiography / ABGs
  • The femoral vein (medial to the pulse) is used for central access & blood sampling
  • Femoral hernia = through the femoral canal, below & lateral to the pubic tubercle (vs inguinal: above & medial); commoner in women, high strangulation risk
The Popliteal Fossa
Borders & contents
  • Diamond: biceps femoris (superolateral); semimembranosus/tendinosus (superomedial); the two gastrocnemius heads (inferior)
  • Contents deep → superficial: popliteal artery (deepest, on the floor) → popliteal vein → tibial nerve (most superficial)
  • The common fibular nerve runs along the lateral border (on biceps tendon) before winding round the fibular neck
Clinical
  • Because the artery is deepest, the popliteal pulse is hard to feel (flex the knee to relax the fascia)
  • Knee dislocation / posterior trauma → popliteal artery injury (tethered at the adductor hiatus & soleal arch) — a limb-threatening emergency
  • Popliteal aneurysm — the commonest peripheral aneurysm (often bilateral, associated with AAA); Baker’s cyst is a common swelling
Compartment Syndrome of the Leg

The leg has four osteofascial compartments; the anterior is the most commonly affected.

CompartmentNerveAction lost
AnteriorDeep fibularDorsiflexion & toe extension
LateralSuperficial fibularEversion
Superficial posteriorTibialPlantarflexion (gastrocnemius/soleus)
Deep posteriorTibialInversion & toe flexion
Acute compartment syndrome. Classically after a tibial fracture or crush/reperfusion. Rising pressure → ischaemia → the 6 Ps (Pain out of proportion & on passive stretch — the earliest sign; Paraesthesia; Pallor; Pulselessness [late]; Paralysis; Perishingly cold). It is a clinical diagnosis → emergency fasciotomy; do not wait for a lost pulse.
Veins — Varicose Veins & DVT
The saphenous veins
  • Great (long) saphenous vein — passes anterior to the medial malleolus (reliable venous cut-down site), up the medial leg & thigh to the saphenofemoral junction; used as a bypass / CABG graft
  • The saphenous nerve runs with it below the knee — at risk during stripping/harvesting
  • Small (short) saphenous vein — behind the lateral malleolus → popliteal vein; runs with the sural nerve
Varicose veins & DVT
  • Varicose veins — incompetent valves (esp. at the SFJ & perforators) → dilated tortuous superficial veins
  • DVT — Virchow’s triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability); usually calf veins; risk of pulmonary embolism
  • Perforating veins connect the superficial to the deep system (one-way valves)
The Knee — Ligaments & the Unhappy Triad
The four ligaments
  • ACL — prevents anterior draw of the tibia; tested by the anterior drawer / Lachman
  • PCL — prevents posterior draw; posterior drawer / sag sign
  • MCL — resists valgus; LCL — resists varus
The unhappy triad
  • A lateral blow to the planted knee tears three structures: ACL + MCL + medial meniscus
  • The medial meniscus is more often injured — it is firmly attached to the MCL
  • Presents with effusion, locking & instability
⭐ Exam Pearls
Common fibular nerve = the most commonly injured nerve in the lower limb (fibular neck) → foot drop.
Intracapsular NOF fracture threatens the femoral-head blood supply (medial femoral circumflex) → AVN.
Trendelenburg: the pelvis drops on the side opposite the weak (stance-leg) gluteus medius — “sound side sags”.
Femoral triangle NAVEL (lateral→medial); the nerve is outside the femoral sheath; pulse at the mid-inguinal point.
Femoral hernia = below & lateral to the pubic tubercle; inguinal hernia = above & medial.
Popliteal artery is the deepest structure → weak pulse; at risk in knee dislocation.
Compartment syndrome is clinical — pain on passive stretch is the earliest sign; fasciotomy before the pulse disappears.
Unhappy triad = ACL + MCL + medial meniscus; give IM injections in the upper-outer quadrant to avoid the sciatic nerve.
LOWER LIMB__Osteology & Joints:
Why this matters: the lower limb is built for weight-bearing and stability, not the mobility of the upper limb — so its bones are heavier, its joints deeper, and its ligaments stronger. Learn the landmarks (every muscle and ligament hangs off one) and the joint design (a deep hip socket, a locking knee, an ankle mortise), and you can reason out the movements, the stability and the fractures.
The Skeleton — Overview
Pelvic girdle
  • Hip bone (os coxae) — ilium + ischium + pubis, fused at the acetabulum
  • Transfers body weight from the axial skeleton to the limb via the sacroiliac joint
Free limb
  • Thigh: femur (+ patella)
  • Leg: tibia (medial, weight-bearing) & fibula (lateral)
  • Foot: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges
The Hip Bone (Os Coxae)

Three bones fuse at the cup-shaped acetabulum: the ilium (superior), ischium (posteroinferior) and pubis (anteroinferior).

Key landmarks
  • Iliac crest → ends as ASIS (front) & PSIS (back); AIIS & PIIS below
  • Greater & lesser sciatic notches, separated by the ischial spine
  • Ischial tuberosity — the “sit bone” (hamstring origin)
  • Pubic tubercle & crest; superior & inferior pubic rami; the obturator foramen
Clinical
  • The ischial spine converts the greater sciatic notch into the greater sciatic foramen via the sacrospinous ligament
  • The ASIS (inguinal ligament, sartorius) & iliac crest (bone marrow biopsy) are palpable landmarks
  • Pelvic fractures risk major haemorrhage & bladder/urethral injury
Femur
RegionLandmarks
ProximalHead (with the fovea for ligamentum teres), neck, greater & lesser trochanters, intertrochanteric line (front) & crest (back)
ShaftLinea aspera (posterior ridge — adductor/vasti attachments), gluteal tuberosity, pectineal line
DistalMedial & lateral condyles & epicondyles, adductor tubercle, patellar surface, intercondylar fossa
The neck–shaft angle. Normally ~125°, angling the shaft medially so the knees sit under the body’s centre of gravity. Coxa vara (<120°) and coxa valga (>135°) alter gait and load. The femoral neck is also anteverted ~15°.
Patella, Tibia & Fibula
Patella & tibia
  • Patella — the largest sesamoid bone (in the quadriceps tendon); it improves the quadriceps lever arm
  • Tibia — the weight-bearing bone: medial & lateral condyles, intercondylar eminence, tibial tuberosity (patellar ligament), sharp anterior border (shin), soleal line, medial malleolus
Fibula
  • Head, neck (common fibular nerve winds here), shaft, lateral malleolus
  • Not weight-bearing — it is for muscle attachment, the lateral malleolus & the ankle mortise; can be harvested as a bone graft
Bones of the Foot

Seven tarsals, five metatarsals and fourteen phalanges. Learn the tarsals with “Tiger Cubs Need MILC” — Talus, Calcaneus, Navicular, and the Cuboid + Medial/Intermediate/Lateral cuneiforms.

Talus — transmits body weight to the foot; has no muscle attachments; its blood supply is retrograde → # risks AVN.
Calcaneus — the largest tarsal (heel); the sustentaculum tali supports the talus; Achilles tendon inserts here.
Navicular — keystone-adjacent on the medial side; tuberosity for tibialis posterior.
Cuboid & 3 cuneiforms — the distal row articulating with the metatarsals.

Metatarsals 1–5 (the 1st is short & stout for weight-bearing); the great toe has 2 phalanges, each other toe has 3.

The Hip Joint

A multiaxial ball-and-socket joint built for stability — the opposite trade-off to the shoulder.

Stability
  • The deep acetabulum is further deepened by the fibrocartilaginous labrum — it grips more than half the head
  • Strong capsule & three reinforcing ligaments make dislocation uncommon (cf. the shoulder)
  • The iliofemoral ligament (Y-shaped) is the strongest ligament in the body — it limits hyperextension
  • Pubofemoral (limits abduction/extension) & ischiofemoral (limits medial rotation) ligaments complete the sleeve
Blood supply & the fovea
  • Mostly the medial femoral circumflex artery → retinacular vessels (torn in intracapsular NOF # → AVN)
  • The artery of the ligamentum teres runs to the fovea — significant in children, minor in adults
  • Movements: flexion (iliopsoas), extension (glut max, hamstrings), abduction (glut med/min), adduction, rotation
The Knee Joint

The largest joint in the body — a modified hinge (bicondylar) combining the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral articulations. Stability comes almost entirely from ligaments & muscles, not bone.

Menisci & ligaments
  • Menisci deepen the tibial plateau & absorb shock; the medial meniscus is C-shaped, less mobile & attached to the MCL → more often torn
  • Cruciates (intracapsular): ACL resists anterior tibial draw; PCL resists posterior draw
  • Collaterals: MCL resists valgus, LCL resists varus
Locking & unlocking
  • Screw-home mechanism: in terminal extension the tibia laterally rotates on the femur, locking the knee for effortless standing
  • Popliteus unlocks it — it medially rotates the tibia (or laterally rotates the femur) to begin flexion
  • Bursae (suprapatellar, prepatellar, infrapatellar) can inflame (“housemaid’s/clergyman’s knee”)
The Ankle & Tibiofibular Joints
The mortise
  • The tibia (plafond + medial malleolus) & fibula (lateral malleolus) form a mortise that grips the talus
  • Held together by the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis — disrupted in Weber C fractures
  • Most stable in dorsiflexion — the talus is wider anteriorly and wedges into the mortise (so most sprains occur in plantarflexion)
Ligaments & the subtalar joint
  • Medial (deltoid) ligament — strong; resists eversion (severe eversion avulses the medial malleolus rather than tearing it)
  • Lateral ligament — ATFL, CFL, PTFL; resists inversion; the ATFL is the most commonly injured in an inversion sprain
  • The subtalar joint produces inversion & eversion
Arches of the Foot

Three arches distribute weight and act as a shock-absorbing spring: two longitudinal and one transverse.

Medial longitudinal arch — the highest; calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms & metatarsals 1–3.
Lateral longitudinal arch — flatter; calcaneus, cuboid & metatarsals 4–5.
Transverse arch — across the cuneiforms & metatarsal bases.
Support: bone shape + ligaments (spring [plantar calcaneonavicular], long/short plantar, plantar aponeurosis) + muscles (tibialis posterior, intrinsics).
Fallen & high arches. Pes planus (flat foot) — loss of the medial arch, often from spring-ligament / tibialis-posterior failure. Pes cavus — an abnormally high arch, sometimes neurological (e.g. Charcot–Marie–Tooth). The plantar aponeurosis is the key passive tie-beam; its inflammation is plantar fasciitis.
🧠 Mnemonics
Tarsal bones — “Tiger Cubs Need MILC” (Talus, Calcaneus, Navicular, Cuboid, Medial/Intermediate/Lateral cuneiforms).
Hip ligaments — iliofemoral (strongest, Y-shaped, limits extension), pubofemoral, ischiofemoral.
Lateral ankle ligaments — “Always Comes Back (Torn)”: ATFL, CFL, PTFL — ATFL most injured.
Joint types — hip = ball-and-socket; knee & ankle = hinge; subtalar = plane; pubic symphysis = secondary cartilaginous.
⭐ Exam Pearls
The iliofemoral ligament is the strongest ligament in the body and limits hip hyperextension.
The hip is deep & stable (rarely dislocates); the shoulder is shallow & mobile (often dislocates) — opposite trade-offs.
Femoral neck–shaft angle ~125°; coxa vara <120°, coxa valga >135°.
Screw-home: the knee locks by lateral rotation of the tibia in extension; popliteus unlocks it.
Medial meniscus is attached to the MCL → torn more often (and together in the unhappy triad).
The ankle is most stable in dorsiflexion (wide anterior talus); sprains happen in plantarflexion + inversion → ATFL.
Deltoid (medial) ligament is strong → eversion tends to avulse the medial malleolus rather than tear it.
Talus has no muscle attachments and a retrograde blood supply → fracture risks avascular necrosis (like the scaphoid).
